1099.quote: water craft akála – outrigger canoe akála aapa [kala:pa] in allegro speech ... mast maleerra The /ee/ here represents [malæ:ra]; primary word stress is on V2. ... FI is a language whose morphophonology is very much built for managing modulations of speed of utterance. It may be said that the language is also built for speed per se. 1106.dq: Stress in Fuyug is predictable. It occurs on the ultimate syllable in two-syllable words (before affixation) and on the antepenultimate in three- and four-syllable words (again, before affixation). [Intonation is treated separately in 2.7: 'Intonation patterns (for statements, incomplete sentences, interrogation, emotions, listing, and calling) are shown in the following subsections.']

1106.prule: Predictable, quantity-insensitive: stress on the ultimate syllable of two-syllable words and on the antepenultimate syllable of three- and four-syllable words, computed on the stem before affixation; affixation does not move stress (so affixed forms can surface with other positions, e.g. 'SS ge-ge, 'SSSS hindel+ele). 1113.tone: Hyman & Katamba 2010 describe Luganda purely tonally (underlying /H, Ø/, intermediate H/L/Ø, surface H/L; mora = TBU; one H-to-L pitch drop per /H/ word) and never mention stress. The 'at most one pitch drop per word' property is why earlier work analysed the system accentually: Heny 1974 'Ganda tone as pitch accent', Hyman 1982 'Globality and the accentual analysis of Luganda tone' (both cited p. 97), and McCawley 1978:126 as quoted in Hyman 2006 (Word-prosodic typology, cached locally, fn. 1): Luganda 'can be described as having a pitch accent system in its deep phonology and a tonal system in its surface phonology.' Either way the prominence is an indication of pitch whose location is lexical, not a stress rule. Crabtree 1902's 'accent is on the penultimate' plausibly reflects the automatic word-final H -> HL fall / phrase-final lengthening heard by a missionary ear; it is not adopted by any modern description reached.

1116.dq: To the extent that Garo can be said to have stress at all, it is relatively independent of the segmental phonology and relatively closely tied to the larger patterns of intonation. In particular, what I will call "stress" helps to define the boundaries of a word.
1116.dloc: Burling 2004 Vol. I, ch. THREE 'Juncture and Prosody', section 'Word Stress (B)', pp. 58-64 (quod.lib.umich.edu div 1:7, read via the Internet Archive 20240731021331)
1116.prule: Non-contrastive word stress. Unsuffixed words (nouns, compounds, numerals, reduplicated adverbs): main stress on the final syllable. Suffixed words: stress stays on the stem-final syllable unless followed by a stress-attracting suffix, in which case it falls on the last stress-attracting suffix. Attracting: verb derivational suffixes (uniformly), most inflectional suffixes, tense-aspect -jok/-na-jok, future -no-(a) (on -no-), plural -drang, reflexive -tang, -kon. Non-attracting: case clitics (-o, -ko, -ni, -cha), neutral tense -a, nominative -a, progressive -ing-, subordinating -e/-e-ming, nominalizing -gip-a/-a, adverbial -e, -na, -ma, -ming. Position is therefore set by suffix identity, not syllable count.
1116.srule: Weaker (non-primary) stresses are morphological, not rhythmic: a weaker stress on the first member of noun compounds (bòl-bi-ják 'tree leaf': heaviest on the final syllable, weaker on the first, least on the second; first members of longer compounds keep some of their own stress, Pi-pròt-ki'-sáng); in suffixed verbs whose main stress is drawn to a word-final tense-aspect suffix, a weak stress remains on the stem-final (last pre-ing stress-bearing) syllable (dak-jà-ing-jók, dak-chàk-ja-ing-jók; Burling: 'I am not fully confidant of my judgment here'); reduplicated adverbs keep residual stress at the end of the first half (hèng-e-héng-e). No alternating/rhythmic secondary stress is described; in long verbs the pattern is 'very difficult to judge'.

1121.prule: Stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (suffixation shifts stress rightward off the root penult; word-final identical-vowel coalescence across a morpheme boundary yields a single stressed surface-final vowel, e.g. /kolu-u/ > /ko'lu/).
1121.srule: Not mentioned in Crowley 2002 (section 1.3 'Stress', p. 526; whole sketch pp. 525-537 read)
1121.quote: 1.3 Stress Stress is applied to the penultimate syllable of the word. With the addition of morphological material after a root, the penultimate syllable of the actual root may be unstressed. When two identical vowels arise word-finally with an intervening morpheme boundary, the resulting sequence is pronounced as a single stressed vowel. Thus compare /'tolu/ ‘three’ with /kolu-u/ ‘with me’ > /ko'lu/.

evidence_works.detail: The article states that Gela word stress generally falls on the penultimate syllable, that morphemes added after the root can leave the penultimate unstressed, and that stressed syllables have higher F0, higher intensity and longer duration; its own acoustic measurements on 76 tokens from 6 male speakers show a sharp pitch movement on the penultimate (stressed) syllable at constituent right edges. The stress rule itself is credited to Crowley 2002, the catalog's existing source, so the article confirms the penultimate entry and adds phonetic correlates and a suffixation exception.

evidence_works.detail: Penultimate stress on the whole word including suffixes (the root's own penult loses stress under suffixation). Secondary stress not mentioned; no weight statement (no contrastive vowel length, sec. 1.1; syllable canon (C)V, sec. 1.2); tone not mentioned anywhere in the sketch.
